claims.text: Land use in a city sorts into zones: the CBD, the commercial centre with offices, shops and high land values; the inner-city areas of older, denser housing that grew when workers walked to work; the suburbs of newer, lower-density housing; and the rural-urban fringe, the zone at the edge of a city where urban and rural land uses meet and farming gives way to new estates.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The CBD holds the highest land values because it is the most accessible point for the most people, so the buildings that pay for it are high-rise, and the ground floor is worth shops, banks and offices, not car parks, while the residential population is small because few can afford to live there.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Land use changes with time and cost: cities grow outwards as their populations grow, so industry and housing push into the rural-urban fringe; older inner-city areas age as their buildings wear out; and a CBD can also lose trade to out-of-town shopping centres, which means urban land use is a snapshot of a process, never a fixed pattern.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Urban problems grow from density and growth: traffic congestion, because many trips converge on one centre; housing shortages and squatter settlements, because arrivals outnumber the homes built; pressure on water supply, sewerage and refuse, which outgrow their pipes and trucks; and loss of farmland at the fringe, because the city spreads onto it.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Solutions work by managing the flow or adding the supply: more roads and bypasses redirect traffic, while public transport moves more people per road-space than cars; serviced land, upgrading of existing settlements and self-help housing schemes close the housing gap; and green belts and planned expansion protect farmland at the fringe.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Windhoek, Namibia's capital, holds about 486 000 people (2023) on its plateau basin at about 1 650 metres, and its growth sorts the land use plainly: the CBD of Independence Avenue with its offices and high-rise shops, the older dense suburbs such as Katutura to the north-west, the low-density southern and eastern suburbs, and the fast-growing informal settlements such as Havana and Okahandja Park at the northern fringe.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Windhoek's problems and answers are Namibia's own: the northern informal settlements grew faster than services, so households faced water points shared between many families and long waits for taxis; the city's answers include the mass-housing and serviced-land programmes launched from 2014, the Shack Dwellers Federation of Namibia, which since the 1990s has helped thousands of families secure land and build homes at well below market cost, and the move of offices and malls towards the fringe, which the southern bypass road now connects.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Windhoek's traffic answers show the two families of solutions: the city built bypasses and ring roads to take through-traffic out of the CBD, and its MoveWindhoek plan, adopted in the 2010s, proposes bus rapid transit and better pavements so that fewer journeys need a private car.
